title: The Agent-Ready Score: 16 Questions That Tell You If Your Internal AI Ops Tool Survives Past Day 30
subtitle: For $1-10M service firm owners and ops leads who want to put an AI tool on the ops they already run. Pick one process, score it, find out where it breaks before you build.

methodology_anchor.name: Agent-Ready Ops
preconditions: Structured input data. The data entering this process is clean enough to be the input layer for an automated decision.
Documentable decision logic. The rules a person follows inside this process can be written down explicitly.
Narrow initial scope. The first cut handles a single decision in a single workflow, not the whole process at once.
Human-in-the-loop by design. Every output passes a person before it ships externally.
methodology_anchor.intro: This assessment scores one process against the four preconditions for Agent-Ready Ops, plus the visibility you need before any of them count. Hit all four and the process can carry an AI tool. Miss one and the tool leaks until someone rips it out.

proof_card.sample_top_leak: decision logic that lives in one person's head (~9 hrs/week stuck on them)

answers.label: Solo or under 10 people. I do most of the ops myself.
11 to 25 people. A small ops layer, founder still in the weeds.
26 to 50 people. Dedicated ops roles, processes mostly written down.
51 to 100 people. Multiple teams, ops is its own function.

questions.text: How completely have you mapped this process from first trigger to final output?

answers.label: 1. Never mapped. It lives in people's heads.
2. A rough idea, nothing written.
3. The main steps are written, gaps remain.
4. Mapped end to end, reviewed once.
5. Mapped, reviewed, and kept current.

questions.text: How well do you know the unofficial steps (the side spreadsheets, the manual fixes, the Slack pings) that keep this process running?

answers.label: 1. No idea what happens off-script.
2. I know a few workarounds exist.
3. I've spotted the big ones.
4. I've sat with the team and logged most.
5. The real workflow, workarounds included, is documented.

questions.text: How clearly defined are the handoffs between the people who touch this process?

answers.label: 1. No one knows who owns what.
2. Handoffs happen by habit, not rule.
3. Roles are clear, triggers are fuzzy.
4. Each handoff has a clear owner and trigger.
5. Handoffs are defined, logged, and rarely dropped.

low.headline: You're flying blind on the process itself
low.text: You can't automate a process no one has walked end to end. Right now the real workflow lives in heads and side spreadsheets, which means an AI tool would automate the version on paper, not the one that actually runs. Map it first.
steps: Sit with the person who runs this process for 60 minutes and watch them do it live.
Write every step, including the workarounds they don't mention until you ask.
Mark each handoff: who triggers it, who receives it, what gets passed.

mid.headline: The map exists, the edges are blurry
mid.text: You've got the main path written, but the gaps are where an AI tool will break. The unofficial fixes and the fuzzy handoff triggers are exactly the spots that cause silent failures. Close those before you build.
steps: Walk the gaps with the team and log the workarounds you haven't captured.
Define the exact trigger for each handoff, not just the owner.
Run the process once on paper and flag every step that needed a judgment call.

high.headline: Visibility is solid. Keep it from going stale.
high.text: You know the real process, workarounds and all. Keep sharpening. The frontier here is keeping the map current as the process drifts, because a six-month-old map quietly stops matching reality.
steps: Set a quarterly review to re-walk the process and catch drift.
Tag the two or three steps most likely to change and watch them.
Hand the map to someone outside the process and see if they can follow it.

operator_brief.headline_number: ~6 hrs/week lost to people re-explaining a process no one wrote down
operator_brief.lever: My read: map the process end to end with the person who runs it before you spend a dollar on tooling.
talking_points: We are about to automate a process we've never documented, which means we'd automate guesses.
The workarounds the team built are part of the real process and they're invisible to leadership.
A two-hour mapping session de-risks the entire build more than any tool choice will.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Spend one week shadowing the process and produce a single end-to-end map; the gaps you find are the build risk.

questions.text: How structured is the data that enters this process?

answers.label: 1. Free-text email and whatever clients send.
2. A form, but most fields are optional or skipped.
3. A form with required fields, loosely enforced.
4. Structured intake, validated on entry.
5. Clean structured data, validated and consistent every time.

questions.text: How often does this process start with complete, correct information?

answers.label: 1. Almost never. We chase missing info constantly.
2. Often incomplete, someone fills gaps later.
3. Usually complete, occasional chasing.
4. Complete most of the time, gaps are rare.
5. Complete and correct on arrival, almost always.

questions.text: How consolidated is the information this process depends on?

answers.label: 1. Scattered across email, Slack, drives, and people's laptops.
2. Spread across 4+ tools, no clear home.
3. Mostly in 2 or 3 systems.
4. One main source, a couple of feeders.
5. One source of truth the whole process reads from.

low.headline: Garbage in, broken tool out
low.text: Your process starts on free-text and scattered data, so an AI tool would spend its life guessing at missing fields and hallucinating the rest. The data pipeline is the bottleneck here, not the AI. Fix the intake before anything else.
steps: Replace the free-text intake with a structured form that requires the fields the process actually needs.
List every system the process reads from and pick one to be the source of truth.
Add a simple completeness check that flags missing data before the work starts.

mid.headline: Structured, but leaking at the edges
mid.text: You've got a form and a couple of systems, but optional fields and scattered sources still let bad data through. An AI tool will amplify whatever inconsistency you feed it. Tighten validation and consolidate before you build.
steps: Make the fields the process depends on required, not optional.
Consolidate the two or three feeder systems into one the tool can read.
Validate inputs on entry so gaps get caught at the door, not downstream.

high.headline: Clean inputs. You're ahead of most.
high.text: Structured, validated, consolidated. That's the precondition most firms skip. Keep sharpening. The frontier is keeping data clean as volume grows and new edge cases enter the pipe.
steps: Add monitoring that flags when input quality dips below your normal baseline.
Document the validation rules so they survive the next hire.
Pressure-test the intake with a deliberately messy entry and see what slips.

operator_brief.headline_number: ~8 hrs/week recoverable from chasing and re-keying incomplete inputs
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: fix the intake form and pick one source of truth before touching any AI tool.
talking_points: We lose hours every week chasing data that should have arrived complete the first time.
Our information is spread across too many systems for any tool to read reliably.
Cleaning the input layer pays back even if we never build the AI tool.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Rebuild the intake as one structured, validated form and run it for a week; measure how many gaps it catches at the door.

questions.text: How well documented are the decisions a person makes inside this process?

answers.label: 1. Not at all. It's gut feel and experience.
2. The person could explain it, nothing is written.
3. The common cases are written, the rest is judgment.
4. Most decisions follow documented rules.
5. Every decision maps to an explicit, written rule.

questions.text: How consistently would two trained people make the same call on the same input?

answers.label: 1. Different people, different answers every time.
2. Roughly aligned on the obvious cases.
3. Same call most of the time, edge cases split.
4. Same call almost always.
5. Identical calls, because the rule is explicit.

questions.text: How clearly are the exceptions and edge cases in this process defined?

answers.label: 1. We handle them ad hoc, every time.
2. We know the common ones, no rules for them.
3. The frequent edge cases have a defined path.
4. Most exceptions route to a clear next step.
5. Edge cases are defined, with a rule or a handoff for each.

low.headline: The logic lives in one person's head
low.text: If your best person can't write down how they decide, you can't encode it, and an AI tool will produce confident wrong answers. This is tacit knowledge that has to become explicit rules first. That's the work that makes the tool possible.
steps: Have the person who owns this process narrate 20 real decisions out loud while you write the why.
Turn the patterns into if-then rules for the common cases.
Mark the decisions that genuinely need judgment and plan to route those to a human.

mid.headline: Common cases are clear, the edges aren't
mid.text: You've documented the predictable decisions, but the edge cases still run on judgment and two people would split on them. That inconsistency is what an AI tool can't reproduce. Define the edges or route them out.
steps: List the edge cases that caused rework in the last month and write a rule for each.
For decisions you can't rule-ify, define a clean handoff to a person.
Test consistency: give two people the same five inputs and compare their calls.

high.headline: Logic is explicit. That's rare.
high.text: Your decisions map to written rules and two people would make the same call. That's the precondition that breaks most AI builds, and you've cleared it. Keep sharpening as new edge cases appear.
steps: Version the decision rules so changes are tracked, not lost.
Capture new edge cases as they surface and fold them into the rule set.
Review the rules quarterly against real cases to catch silent drift.

operator_brief.headline_number: ~9 hrs/week stuck on the one person who 'just knows' how to decide
operator_brief.lever: Honest take: get the decision logic out of one head and into written rules before you automate anything.
talking_points: If our best person leaves, the logic for this process leaves with them.
Two people make different calls on the same input, which means the process isn't actually defined.
Writing the rules down is valuable on its own, before any AI tool exists.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Have your best operator narrate 20 real decisions in a week and turn the patterns into a one-page rule sheet; the gaps you can't fill are the human-review cases.

questions.text: How repeatable is this process week to week?

answers.label: 1. Every instance is basically custom.
2. Loosely similar, lots of variation.
3. A common pattern with frequent exceptions.
4. Mostly the same steps every time.
5. Same steps, same shape, almost every time.

questions.text: How easily could you carve off a single slice of this process to automate first?

answers.label: 1. It's one tangled block, can't separate anything.
2. Hard to split without breaking the rest.
3. I could carve a slice with some effort.
4. There's an obvious slice to start with.
5. A clean, high-volume slice is ready to lift out.

questions.text: How much volume does this process actually carry?

answers.label: 1. A handful of times a month.
2. A few times a week.
3. Daily, moderate volume.
4. Many times a day.
5. High volume, constant, every day.

questions.text: How predictable are the inputs that kick this process off?

answers.label: 1. Wildly different every time.
2. A few common types, lots of one-offs.
3. Mostly predictable, regular surprises.
4. Predictable, occasional outlier.
5. Highly predictable, a known set of input types.

low.headline: Too custom and too quiet to automate yet
low.text: A process that's different every time and runs at low volume won't return its build cost. The 90-Day Payback Rule says this fails the math: the build effort outweighs the hours saved. Find a more repeatable, higher-volume process or narrow this one hard.
steps: Count how many times this runs per week and the minutes each instance takes.
If the volume is low, park this and pick a process that runs daily.
If volume is real, find the single most repeatable slice and scope only that.

mid.headline: Repeatable enough, scope it down
mid.text: There's a pattern here and decent volume, but trying to automate the whole thing on day one means it breaks on edge case number three. Start narrow. Lift out the predictable slice and ship that first.
steps: Identify the 80% of cases that follow the same predictable path.
Scope the first build to that slice only and route the rest to a person.
Confirm the slice carries enough volume to pay back inside 90 days.

high.headline: Repeatable, high-volume, ready to slice
high.text: This runs often, follows a predictable shape, and has a clean slice to start with. That's exactly what a first AI build wants. Keep sharpening by resisting the urge to widen scope too fast.
steps: Ship the narrow high-volume slice first and measure the hours it returns.
Only widen scope once the first slice runs clean for two weeks.
Track payback against the 90-Day rule before approving the next slice.

operator_brief.headline_number: ~12 hrs/week recoverable from the highest-volume slice if scoped narrow
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: start with the single most repeatable, highest-volume slice and ignore the rest on day one.
talking_points: Automating the whole process at once is how these builds break on the first edge case.
The narrow slice has to clear the 90-Day Payback Rule or we don't build it.
High volume on a predictable slice is where the real hours come back.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Pick the one predictable slice that runs daily and run it manually for a week with a stopwatch; the time it eats is your payback case.

questions.text: How clearly defined is the point where a person checks the output before it ships?

answers.label: 1. There's no review step at all.
2. Someone glances at it sometimes.
3. Review happens, no clear standard.
4. A defined review step with a checklist.
5. A clear review gate with criteria and an owner.

questions.text: How quickly would you catch a wrong output today?

answers.label: 1. Only when a client complains.
2. Days later, if we're lucky.
3. Usually within a day.
4. Same day, before it reaches the client.
5. Immediately, the process flags it.

questions.text: How clearly does one person own the quality of this process?

answers.label: 1. No one owns it. Quality is everyone's and no one's.
2. It's shared loosely across the team.
3. One person mostly owns it, unofficially.
4. A named owner, clear responsibility.
5. A named owner with the authority and the metric to back it.

low.headline: No review gate means no safe place to fail
low.text: Without a defined review step, an AI tool's mistakes go straight to clients and you find out when they complain. Human-in-the-loop isn't a sign of failure, it's the design. Build the review gate before you build the tool.
steps: Define the exact point where output gets checked before it leaves the building.
Name one person who owns quality for this process.
Start by routing 100% to review, then dial back as the tool earns trust.

mid.headline: Review exists, but it's informal
mid.text: Someone checks the work, but there's no standard and ownership is fuzzy, so errors still slip through on a bad week. An AI tool needs a defined review gate to be safe to ship. Formalize it.
steps: Turn the informal check into a review step with clear pass-or-fail criteria.
Give the named owner a simple metric for output quality.
Set the review rate at 15 to 20% once the tool is live and stable.

high.headline: Oversight is built in. Ship with confidence.
high.text: You've got a clear review gate, fast error-catching, and a real owner. That's the human-in-the-loop design that lets an AI tool carry weight safely. Keep sharpening by tuning the review rate to the error rate.
steps: Track the error rate so you can lower the review rate as the tool proves out.
Log every caught error to feed back into the decision rules.
Keep the owner accountable to a quality metric, not just a vibe.

operator_brief.headline_number: Errors caught at the client instead of the review gate cost ~3x more to fix
operator_brief.lever: My read: define the review gate and name a quality owner before the tool ships a single output.
talking_points: Routing 15 to 20% of outputs to human review is the design working, not the tool failing.
Right now we'd catch a bad output when a client complains, which is the worst place to find it.
One named owner with a quality metric makes the whole build defensible.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Stand up a one-week review checklist on the current manual process and log every catch; that becomes the gate the AI tool ships through.
